passage:
Volunteer coordinator's note, Saturday. Arohi.
Tenzin, our twenty-year-old intern, ran the welcome desk at the neighbourhood blood-donation camp, and I watched him closely. When old Pandit-ji arrived, Tenzin bent to touch his feet; Pandit-ji beamed. With Dr. Fatima he paused, saw her hand come forward, and shook it. For the two nuns from the convent he simply joined his palms and smiled, and they did the same. A college student got a high five. Afterwards I asked how he decided. He said, 'I just watched what their hands did first.' At the next camp I'll have him train the new volunteers.

qa.q: How did Tenzin greet Dr. Fatima?
qa.a: He saw her hand come forward and shook it.

qa.q: What does Tenzin's answer, 'I just watched what their hands did first', suggest about how he felt at the desk?
qa.a: It suggests he felt calm and attentive rather than anxious about rules, caring more about each person's comfort than a fixed custom.

qa.q: What could new volunteers learn from Tenzin?
qa.a: To pause and read each guest's cue, their hands, age and comfort, before choosing a bow, a handshake or folded hands.

qa.q: How might Dr. Fatima feel when Tenzin waits for her hand before shaking it?
qa.a: She would probably feel respected and at ease, since he followed her lead instead of assuming.

grounding: Shows a young adult choosing between touching feet, a handshake, folded hands or a high five depending on each person, by reading their cue rather than following one fixed rule.

passage:
Sunday, late
Went to Mahima's sister's engagement. Nervous the whole way. At home it's easy: bend, touch feet, done. But Mahima's family is huge and mixed: her Nani is Bengali, her Dadi Punjabi, her Phuphu married into a Goan family. At the door her Dadi opened her arms wide, so I hugged her. Her Nani sat with folded hands, so I did a pranam and got a blessing. Her Goan uncle stuck out his hand: handshake. One very old man I bent toward, and he lifted me by the elbows, laughing, 'No need, no need!' I felt silly for a second, then warm. Next time: watch first, then greet.
Vandana

qa.q: Who stuck out a hand for a handshake?
qa.a: Mahima's Goan uncle.

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling on the way to the engagement?
qa.a: Vandana felt nervous, unsure which greeting would suit each person in such a mixed family.

qa.q: What rule did Vandana end up with, and why is it wise?
qa.a: 'Watch first, then greet', because reading each person's cue is kinder than applying one fixed custom.

qa.q: How might the very old man have felt when Vandana bent toward his feet?
qa.a: He seemed touched but didn't want the formality, so he lifted Vandana up laughing, his own warm way of accepting the respect.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult choosing between touching feet, folded hands, a hug or a handshake by reading each elder's cue in a mixed gathering.

passage:
Field supervisor's note, village survey near Barmer, day 2 — Sudha

Ujjwal (20, intern) handled greetings better than I expected.

At the first house, an old farmer reached out a hand to bless him; Ujjwal bent and touched his feet, and the man beamed. At the next house the elder was Muslim; Ujjwal put his hand to his chest and said "Adaab," matching what the man offered. The panchayat secretary, a young woman, kept her hands folded, so he folded his instead of reaching out. With the visiting donor from Sweden, a firm handshake.

When I asked how he chose, he said, "I watch what they start with, and follow."

What I did next: I asked him to brief the other interns tonight.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal say to the Muslim elder?
qa.a: Ujjwal said "Adaab," matching what the man offered.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal's answer 'I watch what they start with' suggest about his mindset?
qa.a: It suggests he is respectful and curious about each person, wanting them to feel comfortable rather than following one fixed rule.

qa.q: What could the other interns learn from Ujjwal?
qa.a: Watch the other person's cue first, whether a blessing, folded hands, adaab or a handshake, and match it.

qa.q: How might the panchayat secretary feel when Ujjwal folds his hands instead of reaching out?
qa.a: She likely feels respected and at ease, since he followed her choice of greeting.

grounding: Shows a young adult choosing between touching feet, adaab, namaste and a handshake by reading each person's cue, noted by a supervisor.

passage:
Saturday night.

Went to Irawati's for the Ganesh puja today and spent the whole auto ride panicking about greetings. Do I touch her Ajoba's feet? I'm Muslim; would it look fake? Would NOT doing it look rude?

In the end I just watched. Ajoba came to the door and held out his hand, so I shook it with both hands, and he laughed and patted my shoulder. Her Aaji stood back with her hands folded, so I folded mine and said namaste. Her little cousin ran at me for a high-five.

Four people, three greetings, zero disasters.

Irawati said later, "You were so stiff at the door!" True. But nobody felt awkward except me, and that's fine.

Wasim

qa.q: What did Ajoba do at the door?
qa.a: Ajoba came to the door and held out his hand.

qa.q: How was Wasim feeling on the auto ride?
qa.a: Wasim felt anxious and torn, worried that touching feet might look fake and that not doing it might look rude.

qa.q: What approach worked for Wasim?
qa.a: Watching each person's cue and matching it: a handshake for Ajoba, namaste for Aaji, a high-five for the little cousin.

qa.q: How might Ajoba see the two-handed handshake?
qa.a: Ajoba seemed pleased and amused, laughing and patting Wasim's shoulder.

grounding: Shows a young adult of another faith choosing each greeting at a friend's home by reading the other person's cue instead of one fixed rule.

Yamini: so? say hi

Yamini: they're Christian, na? she might find it odd

Manjula: so I held hers back and said thank you, Ammachi, Grace talks about you all the time

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling before going in?
qa.a: Manjula felt nervous and unsure, torn between touching feet as at home and worrying it might seem odd.

qa.q: What advice did Yamini give, and why did it work?
qa.a: Watch what the grandmother does first and match it; following her cue let the greeting feel natural to both.

qa.q: How might Grace's grandma have felt about Manjula's greeting?
qa.a: She likely felt warmly respected, which is why she invited Manjula to sit with her for the cake.

passage:
Devika, twenty-one, had come to Tejas's village near Nashik for his sister's wedding, and she had no rule book. At the gate, Tejas's grandmother sat on a cot. Devika bent towards her feet; the old woman smiled and blessed her, pleased. Next came Tejas's uncle's friend, Jameel chacha, in a white skullcap. Devika hesitated, then placed her hand on her chest and nodded. He smiled and said, "Adaab, beti." Then a young woman doctor from the district hospital held out her hand. Devika shook it firmly.
Later, a very old man at the wedding stepped back when she began to bend. "No, no, namaste is enough," he said, hands folded. She folded hers too. Tejas laughed. "How do you know what to do?" Devika shrugged. "I don't. I just watch what they seem comfortable with." He noticed his grandmother nodding approvingly from the cot.

qa.q: How did Devika greet the young woman doctor?
qa.a: She shook her hand firmly.

qa.q: How did Devika feel arriving without a rule book, and how did she handle it?
qa.a: She felt unsure and a little hesitant, but calm enough to watch each person and follow their comfort.

qa.q: Why is Devika's way of greeting polite?
qa.a: She reads each person's cue, their age, faith and comfort, rather than using one fixed rule, so everyone feels respected.

qa.q: How might Tejas's grandmother see Devika?
qa.a: She probably approves of Devika, pleased by the respect shown to her and to the others, as her nod suggests.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult choosing between touching feet, a handshake or namaste depending on each person's age, faith and comfort.
